_comment: Per-role scope and weight, authored in UHS and merged by scripts/port-livelihoods.ts. The ported table has none of this: every trade was available in every era the tier allowed, everywhere on Earth, at the same frequency as every other. `years` is half-open and astronomical. `weight` is a relative share of the workforce, default 1; a value of 20 on a cultivator against 1 on a glazier is what makes a village mostly farmers. `bounds`, `cultures` and `ecologies` narrow work that is local. Phase 2 fills this in; Phase 1 only wires it up, with the dates that were previously hidden inside the tier test.

_tierDates.why: The industrial and modern tiers were the only ones that consulted a year, inside the settlement-form test. Moved here so the test is about settlement form alone.

potter.why: Ungated, so offered from the earliest farming date, about two thousand years before ceramics.

glazier.why: Gated only on urban settlement, so available in Uruk around 3500 BCE, some three and a half thousand years before window glass.

cooper.why: Stave barrels are Iron Age Celtic and spread from there. Ungated it appeared in Bronze Age Mesopotamia and in Mesoamerica and the Andes, which had neither barrels nor the cooperage tradition.

saddler.why: Gated only on draft animals, so from 3500 BCE; saddles are later. Follows the working horse.

miller.why: A miller presupposes a mill. Grinding by quern is household work, not a trade.

charcoal-burner.why: Charcoal as a specialised trade follows smelting rather than preceding it. Charcoal burning as a living ends with coke smelting and bottled gas.

peat-cutter.why: Already bounded in phase 1; kept here with the rest.

thresher.why: Hand threshing with a flail ends with the threshing machine. Hand threshing with a flail ends with the threshing machine.

cottager.why: A tenure of cottage and common rights, ended by enclosure and the wage.

shepherd.why: Shepherding survives in hill country but stops being an ordinary village job.

goatherd.why: Goat keeping continues; the standing village office does not.

swineherd.why: Pig keeping continues; the word and the job as a separate village office do not.

dairymaid.why: Hand milking as a named household office.

maize-cultivator.why: Maize domestication in Mesoamerica; the Andes adopt it later.

potato-farmer.why: Potatoes are Andean and ancient there, and nowhere else before 1550.

date-cultivator.why: Date palms are cultivated in Mesopotamia and the Gulf from the Bronze Age.

fellah.why: An Arabic term for a peasant cultivator; it belongs to the Islamic-era countryside, not the Neolithic. An Ottoman and colonial-era term for the Egyptian peasantry.

market-gardener.why: Market gardening presupposes a town market buying vegetables daily.

vine-dresser.why: Viticulture spreads with the Mediterranean world. Viticulture continues under other names and arrangements.

dairy-farmer.why: Dairying as a farm's main business rather than a household task.

homesteader.why: A settler tenure of the North American interior.

ranch-hand.why: Ranching follows the introduction of cattle and horses to the Americas.

sharecropper.why: Sharecropping as a named tenure, rather than tenancy in general.

agricultural-labourer.why: Landless wage labour on the land, as against a tenancy.

coffee-picker.why: Coffee reaches the Americas as a plantation crop in the eighteenth century.

tea-picker.why: Commercial tea picking as wage work in South Asia follows the Assam plantations.

tea-grower.why: Tea cultivation in China is Tang-era and later.

jute-grower.why: Jute as a cash crop follows the Dundee trade.

groundnut-grower.why: Groundnuts are an American crop grown for export in the Sahel from the nineteenth century.

cotton-grower.why: Cotton is ancient in South Asia, unlike the plantation crops beside it here.

coca-grower.why: Coca cultivation in the Andes long predates the Spanish.

beekeeper.why: Hive-keeping is attested in Egypt around 2400 BCE; it was previously offered from the first farming villages anywhere on Earth.

candle-maker.why: Tallow and wax candles as a trade are Roman and later.

soap-boiler.why: Soap boiling as a trade is Roman and later.

oil-presser.why: Olive and sesame pressing follows the orchard crops, not the first cereals.

salt-worker.why: Salt production as specialised work, rather than gathering it where it lies.

dyer.why: Dyeing as a trade separate from household cloth work.

sexton.why: A Christian parish office. Gated only on urban settlement it appeared in Uruk, Anyang, Teotihuacan and Cahokia.

alewife.why: An English trade with its own legal regime, the assize of ale. An English trade with its own legal regime, the assize of ale.

publican.why: Innkeeping is ancient; it was locked behind the industrial tier.

stonemason.why: Monumental stone dressing is Bronze Age; it was locked behind the industrial tier.

bricklayer.why: Mud brick and fired brick are both ancient; locked behind the industrial tier.

sailor.why: There was no seafaring livelihood at all before 1780, which left every ancient port without sailors.

night-watchman.why: A town watch is ancient; it was modern-tier only, so no settlement had anyone keeping watch before 1900.

chapman.why: An English and northern European pedlar; it was offered worldwide.

costermonger.why: A London street seller of fruit; it was offered worldwide.

night-soil-collector.why: Urban waste collection follows dense cities. Ends with piped sewerage.

ostler.why: Stabling for travellers' horses ends with the motor car.

cabman.why: The horse cab gives way to the taxi.

muleteer.why: Pack transport gives way to the lorry.

wool-comber.why: Combing is mechanised early in the textile factories.

fuller.why: Fulling by foot and by stock gives way to the fulling mill and then the factory.

scullion.why: The lowest kitchen servant disappears with domestic service itself.

match-worker.why: A trade that existed only while matches were dipped by hand.

lime-burner.why: Field and village lime kilns give way to industrial cement.

rope-maker.why: Hand ropewalks give way to machine spinning.

sawyer.why: Pit sawing by hand ends with the powered sawmill.

wheelwright.why: Wooden wheels for carts and carriages.

errand-boy.why: Child errand work ends with schooling laws.

washerwoman.why: Ends with the domestic washing machine.

drover.why: Driving stock overland on the hoof ends with the railway.

carter.why: Horse haulage gives way to the lorry.

spinner.why: Hand spinning for a living ends with the mule and the throstle.

brickmaker.why: Hand moulding gives way to the brickworks.

scribe.why: Writing for other people as a trade fades as literacy spreads.

thatcher.why: Survives as a heritage trade rather than ordinary work.

extraRoles._comment: Work authored in UHS and emitted alongside the ported table. These are subsistence bases the upstream agrarian table has no entry for, each tied to the country that supports it.

camel-herder.label: Camel Herder
camel-herder.why: Dromedary pastoralism across the Saharan and Arabian deserts; camels are domesticated in Arabia in the second millennium BCE. Bounded to the Saharan, Arabian and central Asian deserts: ecology alone let it into Mediterranean scrub.

reindeer-herder.label: Reindeer Herder
reindeer-herder.why: Sami and Siberian reindeer pastoralism, distinct from hunting wild reindeer, which is far older. Bounded to Fennoscandia and northern Siberia: ecology alone let it onto the Mongolian steppe.

yak-herder.label: Yak Herder
yak-herder.why: Yak pastoralism on the Tibetan plateau and its margins, where nothing else will graze.

horse-herder.label: Horse Herder
horse-herder.why: Horse-keeping on the open steppe, the basis of mounted pastoralism.

swidden-cultivator.label: Swidden Cultivator
swidden-cultivator.why: Shifting cultivation: clear, burn, crop for a few seasons, move on. The commonest form of farming in forested country and invisible in a table that assumes permanent fields. Bounded to the tropics and warm temperate zone.

terrace-farmer.label: Terrace Farmer
terrace-farmer.why: Cutting and maintaining terraces on slopes too steep to plough. Bounded to monsoon and Himalayan Asia; Andean terracing is covered by the Andean roles.

irrigation-keeper.label: Irrigation Keeper
irrigation-keeper.why: Maintaining and allocating the channels, which in irrigated societies is its own job and often its own office.

sea-fisher.label: Sea Fisher
sea-fisher.why: Fishing from a boat off the coast, as against the shore and river work the single existing fisher role covers.

religious-specialist.label: Religious specialist
religious-specialist.why: One row standing for every officiant. The label and its rarity come from the belief system in force here, so Egypt yields a priest of Amun-Ra and 17th-century Germany a Lutheran minister. Societies whose record does not name an officiant produce none.

field-slave.label: Field hand
field-slave.why: Gang labour on the land, the commonest condition of enslaved people in the plantation Americas and a large part of estate agriculture in the classical world. Bounded south of the manorial north, where unfree field labour was villeinage rather than chattel slavery.

household-slave.label: Household servant
household-slave.why: Domestic bondage: cooking, carrying, minding children, attending a household's members.

bound-labourer.label: Bound labourer
bound-labourer.why: Carrying, hauling and building under compulsion, in mines, on docks and at public works.

bondservant.label: Bondservant
bondservant.why: Indenture: bound for a term of years rather than for life, and most of the early English colonial labour force.

villein.label: Villein
villein.why: Bound to the manor and owing labour services on the lord's demesne, as against owned outright.

serf.label: Serf
serf.why: Russian serfdom, which by the eighteenth century allowed sale apart from the land.

warrior.label: Warrior
warrior.why: Fighting as what a man of standing does, rather than as paid service. Ungated: it needs no state to retain him.

retainer.label: Retainer
retainer.why: Kept in arms by a lord or a state. The capability was dated for every culture and gated nothing at all.

town-watchman.label: Watchman
town-watchman.why: A town watch is as old as towns; the only watch roles were modern-tier.

gate-keeper.label: Gate Keeper
gate-keeper.why: Keeping and closing the gate, which is a named office in most walled towns.

armourer.label: Armourer
armourer.why: Making and mending arms and armour.

fletcher.label: Fletcher
fletcher.why: Making arrows, which is separate work from making the bow.

apprentice.label: Apprentice
apprentice.why: Bound to a master for a term of years. The capability existed and gated nothing, so no town had apprentices.

journeyman.label: Journeyman
journeyman.why: Out of apprenticeship, working for wages, not yet a master.

guild-master.label: Guild Master
guild-master.why: Holding the freedom of a craft and the right to take apprentices.

money-changer.label: Money Changer
money-changer.why: Coinage was dated per culture and gated nothing; a place with coin needs someone who knows what it is worth.

headman.label: Headman
headman.why: Speaking for a settlement to whoever is above it, which every settlement needs and none had.

village-elder.label: Village Elder
village-elder.why: Settling disputes and remembering what was agreed.

tax-collector.label: Tax Collector
tax-collector.why: The oldest use writing is put to.

toll-keeper.label: Toll Keeper
toll-keeper.why: Taking the toll at a bridge, a gate or a ford.

musician.label: Musician
musician.why: There was no music, dance or storytelling anywhere in the table, in any era.

storyteller.label: Storyteller
storyteller.why: Holding what a community knows about itself, which in a society without writing is an office.

carver.label: Carver
carver.why: Wood, bone and stone carving, the core craft of several regions the game covers.

boatwright.label: Boatwright
boatwright.why: Building and mending boats, which every water-side settlement needs and none could staff.

salt-panner.label: Salt Panner
salt-panner.why: Evaporating sea water, distinct from mining rock salt.

shopkeeper.label: Shopkeeper
shopkeeper.why: A fixed shop rather than a stall, which is what a high street is made of and what the table had none of.

confectioner.label: Confectioner
confectioner.why: A pastry and sweet shop, distinct from the bread baker.

clerk.label: Clerk
clerk.why: Keeping books and correspondence for a merchant, a bank or an office: the commonest town job of the nineteenth century and absent entirely.

printer.label: Printer
printer.why: From the spread of the press.

policeman.label: Policeman
policeman.why: A uniformed civil police, as against a town watch.

lamplighter.label: Lamplighter
lamplighter.why: Lighting and dousing the street lamps, until electricity.
